title: Multiplicativity of the degree extended by zero
statement: Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure], and let $A/k$ be an abelian variety [def-sc-abelian-variety] of positive dimension. For a group-scheme endomorphism $a:A\to A$ [def-sc-group-scheme], let $d(a)$ be the order of its finite kernel if $a$ is an isogeny, and zero otherwise [def-sc-isogeny]. Then $d(\mathrm{id}_A)=1$ and $d(a\circ b)=d(a)d(b)$ for all endomorphisms $a,b$; no separability assumption is imposed.

source.place: Chapter I §7, printed p.32, identification of isogeny degree with function-field degree; Remark 10.11, printed p.47; multiplicativity used in Lemma 10.22 and Proposition 10.20, printed pp.51–52.

proof.text: The identity has scheme-theoretic kernel $\operatorname{Spec}k$: on every test scheme its kernel consists only of the identity section. It is surjective, hence is an isogeny, and its kernel algebra is $k$, of dimension one. Thus $d(\mathrm{id}_A)=1$.

source.place: Chapter I §7, Proposition 7.1 and following degree paragraph, printed p.32; Remark 10.11, printed p.47.

proof.text: Put $c=a\circ b$. If $c$ is an isogeny, its surjectivity implies that $a$ is surjective. Since source and target are both $A$, [lem-sfb-equal-dimension-isogeny-criterion] makes $a$ an isogeny. Also $\ker b$ is a closed subscheme of $\ker c$: on test schemes $b(x)=0$ implies $a(b(x))=0$; both kernels are closed subgroup schemes of $A$ by [lem-sc-kernel-subgroup]. Explicitly their defining ideals satisfy $\mathcal I_{\ker c}\subseteq\mathcal I_{\ker b}$, since pulling back the equations of the unit along $a\circ b$ gives equations vanishing on $b=0$. As $\ker c=\operatorname{Spec}C$ is finite over $k$, the subscheme $\ker b$ is $\operatorname{Spec}(C/J)$ for an ideal $J$; the quotient of the finite-dimensional vector space $C$ is finite-dimensional. Thus $\ker b$ is finite over $k$. Apply [lem-sfb-finite-kernel-equal-dimension-isogeny] with both varieties equal to $A$ and the given algebraically closed field: $b$ is surjective. Together with its finite kernel, this makes $b$ an isogeny.

source.place: Chapter I §7, Proposition 7.1 and following degree paragraph, printed p.32; Remark 10.11, printed p.47.

proof.text: Conversely, if $a,b$ are isogenies, $a\circ b$ is surjective as a composite of surjective maps, so [lem-sfb-equal-dimension-isogeny-criterion] makes it an isogeny. By [lem-sc-isogeny-degree], the three maps are finite flat, and their structure-sheaf pushforwards have constant ranks $d(a),d(b),d(a\circ b)$. Apply [lem-sfb-finite-kernel-equal-dimension-isogeny] to each map, whose kernel is finite: all three maps are finite locally free. Their finite locally free degrees in [def-pc-finite-locally-free] are the ranks just identified. Apply [lem-sfb-finite-locally-free-degree-composition] to $b$ followed by $a$ to get degree $d(b)d(a)$. Evaluate the two constant degree formulas at the identity point of $A$, which exists by its group structure: $d(a\circ b)=d(b)d(a)=d(a)d(b)$.

source.place: Chapter I §7, Proposition 7.1 and following degree paragraph, printed p.32; Remark 10.11, printed p.47.

proof.text: If either $a$ or $b$ is not an isogeny, step 2 shows that $a\circ b$ is not an isogeny. The defining zero extension therefore gives $d(a\circ b)=0=d(a)d(b)$. This and step 3 cover all pairs. All degrees above are dimensions of finite kernel algebras, so the proof counts scheme length, including inseparable kernels, and never replaces it by the number of geometric points.
